newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: ADB says eager to promote South Asian "quadrangle".
newsitem.headline: ADB says eager to promote South Asian "quadrangle".

text.p: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) said it was eager to help the proposed four-nation South Asian economic cooperation group take concrete shape.

"The dividend of an effective cooperation in this sub-region is beyond imagination. My bank is ready to offer its expertise and resources," the ADB's mission chief in Dhaka, Bhanuphol Horayangura, told Reuters on Thursday.
Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and seven northeastern states of India have agreed to form a sub-regional bloc for closer economic cooperation.

Officials of the four countries, all of whom are already members of the seven-nation South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), are discussing issues on setting up the forum, dubbed the South Asian Growth Quandrangle.
Horanyangura said a high-level mission from the ADB's headquarters in Manila would arrive in Dhaka next week to identify specific projects for the "quadrangle".
The delegation will also visit other countries of the proposed grouping.
"They will specifically look into development of Bangladesh's Chittagong port, transit facilities and power projects," he said.
"Potential for cooperation in hydro-power and other infrastructure areas is tremendous. The cooperation can bring radical changes in the poverty situation in South Asia," the ADB official said.
South Asia is considered one of the world's poorest regions with an impoverished population of around 500 million.
Horayangura said Nepal and India's northeastern state of Meghalaya had the potential for producing 50,000 megawatts of hydro-electricity.

"It's a pity that this vast potential is still untapped and Bangladesh has been spending its natural gas resources merely for producing power. The gas could be used in other areas like producing fertiliser."
He said a regional power grid could allow countries to cut costs by swapping power according to their needs.
The ADB is already funding a technical assistance project to facilitate commercial arrangements in electricity sharing between Bangladesh and India.
Horayangura said Bangladesh could become a financial hub of the sub-region if its ports were developed and opened to cater to landlocked Nepal, Bhutan and seven northeastern Indian states.
"ADB's experience in helping the Mekong sub-region in Southeast Asia is very good. We want to help the South Asia region the same way," he said.
Laos, Vietnam, Cambodia, Burma and China's Yunnan province floated a sub-regional bloc in 1992 for closer cooperation.
ADB and other co-financiers funded a hydro-power project in Laos to meet the electricity needs of Thailand and other countries in the sub-region.
The proposed South Asian Growth Quandrangle has faced resistance from Pakistan which said it was a ploy by New Delhi to destroy SAARC and firm up its grip over the region.
Bangladeshi officials have said Dhaka would move ahead with the plan.
SAARC has remained largely ineffective mostly due to rivalry between India and Pakistan, keeping the intra-SAARC trade at a paltry two percent of the region's total international trade turnover.
